claim: Insects adapt their response to stimuli, such as odours, according to their pairing with positive or negative reinforcements, such as sugar or shock.
source: Insects adapt their response to stimuli, such as odours, according to their pairing with positive or negative reinforcements, such as sugar or shock.
evidence: This is a general statement about insect behavior that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule supports a variety of synaptic strength change phenomena.
source: We propose that this data can be explained by the combination of a dopaminergic plasticity rule that supports a variety of synaptic strength change phenomena, and a circuit structure (derived from neuroanatomy) between dopaminergic and output neurons that creates different roles for specific neurons.
evidence: The authors propose this based on their computational modeling results.

claim: The circuit structure between dopaminergic and output neurons creates different roles for specific neurons.
source: We propose that this data can be explained by the combination of a dopaminergic plasticity rule that supports a variety of synaptic strength change phenomena, and a circuit structure (derived from neuroanatomy) between dopaminergic and output neurons that creates different roles for specific neurons.
evidence: The circuit structure is derived from neuroanatomical data and the model demonstrates different functional roles.

claim: The computational model allows for rapid memory acquisition.
source: Computational modelling shows that this circuit allows for rapid memory acquisition, transfer from short term to long term, and exploration/exploitation trade-off.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: The computational model allows for transfer from short term to long term memory.
source: Computational modelling shows that this circuit allows for rapid memory acquisition, transfer from short term to long term, and exploration/exploitation trade-off.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: The computational model allows for exploration/exploitation trade-off.
source: Computational modelling shows that this circuit allows for rapid memory acquisition, transfer from short term to long term, and exploration/exploitation trade-off.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling results.

claim: The model can reproduce the observed changes in the activity of each of the identified neurons in conditioning paradigms.
source: The model can reproduce the observed changes in the activity of each of the identified neurons in conditioning paradigms and can be used for flexible behavioural control.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model outputs with experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The model can be used for flexible behavioural control.
source: The model can reproduce the observed changes in the activity of each of the identified neurons in conditioning paradigms and can be used for flexible behavioural control.
evidence: This is demonstrated through behavioral simulations in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is able to form, retain, and forget olfactory associations with reinforcements, for example, electric shock.
source: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is able to form, retain, and forget olfactory associations with reinforcements, for example, electric shock.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila neuroscience.

claim: The key neural substrate for olfactory associations in Drosophila lies in the mushroom bodies.
source: The key neural substrate is known to lie in the neuropils of their brain called the mushroom bodies (MBs) (Davis, 1993; Heisenberg, 2003; Busto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There are two mushroom bodies in the insect brain, one in each hemisphere.
source: There are two MBs in the insect brain, one in each hemisphere, composed of intrinsic and extrinsic neurons.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Extrinsic projection neurons deliver sensory input to the Kenyon cells.
source: Extrinsic projection neurons (PN) deliver sensory input to the only intrinsic neurons of the MBs, the Kenyon cells (KCs), whose long parallel axons travel through the pendunculus and then split forming the vertical (α/α′) and medial (β/β′ and γ) MB lobes (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about mushroom body connectivity.

claim: Kenyon cells are the only intrinsic neurons of the mushroom bodies.
source: Extrinsic projection neurons (PN) deliver sensory input to the only intrinsic neurons of the MBs, the Kenyon cells (KCs), whose long parallel axons travel through the pendunculus and then split forming the vertical (α/α′) and medial (β/β′ and γ) MB lobes (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Kenyon cell axons split to form the vertical (α/α′) and medial (β/β′ and γ) mushroom body lobes.
source: Extrinsic projection neurons (PN) deliver sensory input to the only intrinsic neurons of the MBs, the Kenyon cells (KCs), whose long parallel axons travel through the pendunculus and then split forming the vertical (α/α′) and medial (β/β′ and γ) MB lobes (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Mushroom body output neurons extend their dendrites in different regions of the lobes, receiving input from the Kenyon cells and forming 15 distinct compartments.
source: The extrinsic mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) extend their dendrites in different regions of the lobes, receiving input from the KCs and forming 15 distinct compartments (Turner et al., 2008; Tanaka et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to anatomical studies.

claim: MBON activity is thought to provide motivational output that modulates the default behaviour of the animal.
source: Their activity is thought to provide motivational output that modulates the default behaviour of the animal (Aso et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Different groups of dopaminergic neurons terminate their axons in specific compartments of the mushroom body and modulate the connections between Kenyon cells and MBONs.
source: Different groups of extrinsic dopaminergic neurons (DANs) terminate their axons in specific compartments of the MB and modulate the connections between KCs and MBONs (Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Many dopaminergic neurons respond to a variety of reinforcement signals.
source: Many of the DANs respond to a variety of reinforcement signals (Mao and Davis, 2009; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2014), and therefore, they are considered the main source of reinforcement signals in the MB.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons are considered the main source of reinforcement signals in the mushroom body.
source: Many of the DANs respond to a variety of reinforcement signals (Mao and Davis, 2009; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2014), and therefore, they are considered the main source of reinforcement signals in the MB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited functional studies.

claim: Many MBON axons and DAN dendrites meet in convergence zones where they create interconnections.
source: Finally, many of the MBON axons and DAN dendrites meet in the convergence zones (CZs), where they create interconnections, such that the motivational output can also influence the activity of the reinforcement neurons (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: The motivational output can influence the activity of the reinforcement neurons through convergence zone interconnections.
source: Finally, many of the MBON axons and DAN dendrites meet in the convergence zones (CZs), where they create interconnections, such that the motivational output can also influence the activity of the reinforcement neurons (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to functional studies.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule uses the reinforcement to maximise the separation between the synaptic weights of reinforced inputs.
source: Instead of calculating the error between the reinforcement and its prediction, DPR uses the reinforcement to maximise the separation between the synaptic weights of reinforced inputs, which is functionally closer to the information maximisation theory (Bell and Sejnowski, 1995; Lee et al., 1999; Lulham et al., 2011) than the RPE principle.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed plasticity rule and its theoretical basis.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule is functionally closer to information maximisation theory than the reward prediction error principle.
source: Instead of calculating the error between the reinforcement and its prediction, DPR uses the reinforcement to maximise the separation between the synaptic weights of reinforced inputs, which is functionally closer to the information maximisation theory (Bell and Sejnowski, 1995; Lee et al., 1999; Lulham et al., 2011) than the RPE principle.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical relationship of the proposed rule to existing theories.

claim: When the dopaminergic factor is negative and the KC is active, the KC→MBON synaptic weight is decreased (depression effect).
source: If the dopaminergic factor is negative and the KC is active (positive), the KC→MBON synaptic weight is decreased (depression effect of the plasticity rule, see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation of the rule and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: When the dopaminergic factor is positive and the KC is active, the potentiation effect causes an increase in the synaptic weights.
source: When the dopaminergic factor is positive and the KC is active, we have the potentiation effect, which causes an increase in the synaptic weights (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation of the rule and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The saturation effect occurs when the KC is inactive and the dopaminergic factor is positive, enhancing diversity in MBON responses.
source: If the KC is inactive and the dopaminergic factor is positive, then we have the saturation effect, where if the current synaptic weight is higher than its resting weight, the synaptic weight continues to increase, while if it is lower then it continues to decrease (see Figure 2D). This effect enhances diversity in the responses of the MBON to the different past and current CS experiences, which is essential for memory consolidation (i.e., continued strengthening of a memory) and the formation of long-term memories (i.e., slower acquisition and resistance to further change).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation and its functional implications, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: The incentive circuit consists of six MBONs that receive KC input and six DANs that modulate the KC-MBON connections.
source: What we call the IC is a circuit in the MB of the fruit fly D. melanogaster that allows complicated memory dynamics through self-motivation. We have identified and modelled this circuit (shown in Figure 3) which consists of six MBONs that receive KC input and six DANs that modulate the KC-MBON connections.
evidence: This is the description of the proposed model circuit shown in Figure 3.

claim: All the neurons and connections in the incentive circuit are mapped to identified connectivity in the mushroom body.
source: All the neurons and connections in this circuit are mapped to identified connectivity in the MB as summarised in Table 1.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed mapping provided in Table 1.

claim: For each motivation (attraction or avoidance), the incentive circuit has three types of MBON — susceptible, restrained, and LTM — and three types of DAN — discharging, charging, and forgetting.
source: As presented in Figure 3, for each motivation (attraction or avoidance), the IC has three types of MBON — susceptible, restrained, and LTM — and three types of DAN — discharging, charging, and forgetting.
evidence: This is the description of the model structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: Discharging DANs respond to punishment or reward and influence the susceptible MBONs.
source: More specifically, working from the outer edges of the model, we have 'discharging' DANs that respond to punishment (left side) or reward (right side) and influence the 'susceptible' MBONs, which by default respond to all KC inputs (not shown).
evidence: This is a description of the model function.

claim: Susceptible MBONs by default respond to all KC inputs.
source: More specifically, working from the outer edges of the model, we have 'discharging' DANs that respond to punishment (left side) or reward (right side) and influence the 'susceptible' MBONs, which by default respond to all KC inputs (not shown).
evidence: This is a description of the model function.

claim: Susceptible MBONs inhibit the responses of the restrained MBONs of opposite valence.
source: These in turn inhibit the responses of the 'restrained' MBONs of opposite valence.
evidence: This is a description of the model connectivity.

claim: When discharging DANs depress the response of susceptible MBONs of opposite valence, they release the restrained MBONs of the same valence.
source: When the discharging DANs depress the response of the susceptible MBONs of opposite valence, they release the restrained MBONs of the same valence, and also decrease the inhibitory feedback to the discharging DANs from the susceptible MBONs.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: Restrained MBONs activate their respective charging DANs.
source: The restrained MBONs activate their respective 'charging' DANs, which start to potentiate the LTM MBONs of the same valence, while also depressing the response (to KC input) of the restrained MBON of opposite valence.
evidence: This is a description of the model connectivity and dynamics.

claim: Charging DANs potentiate the LTM MBONs of the same valence.
source: The restrained MBONs activate their respective 'charging' DANs, which start to potentiate the LTM MBONs of the same valence, while also depressing the response (to KC input) of the restrained MBON of opposite valence.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: LTM MBONs enhance the activity of the charging DANs, increasing the momentum of LTM.
source: Similarly, the LTM MBONs enhance the activity of the charging DANs, increasing the momentum of LTM, while simultaneously activating their respective 'forgetting' DANs, to decrease the momentum of the opposite valence LTM.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: LTM MBONs activate their respective forgetting DANs to decrease the momentum of the opposite valence LTM.
source: Similarly, the LTM MBONs enhance the activity of the charging DANs, increasing the momentum of LTM, while simultaneously activating their respective 'forgetting' DANs, to decrease the momentum of the opposite valence LTM.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: Forgetting DANs depress the restrained MBONs, making space for the acquisition of new memories while preserving old ones.
source: The forgetting DANs also depress the restrained MBONs, which makes space for the acquisition of new memories while preserving old ones.
evidence: This is a description of the model function.

claim: Pavlowsky et al., 2018 identified a microcircuit where a punishment-encoding DAN (PPL1-γ1pedc) depresses the KC synapses onto an attraction-driving MBON (MBON-γ1pedc>α/β), which in turn inhibits the same DAN.
source: Pavlowsky et al., 2018 identified a microcircuit in the MB, where a punishment-encoding DAN (PPL1-γ1pedc) depresses the KC synapses onto an attraction-driving MBON (MBON-γ1pedc>α/β), which in turn inhibits the same DAN.
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The drop in MBON response reduces its inhibition of the DAN, enhancing the formation of memory if the same odour-punishment pairing is continued.
source: They argue that this is a memory consolidation mechanism as the drop in the MBON response will reduce its inhibition of the DAN, enhancing the formation of the memory if the same odour-punishment pairing is continued.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cited work by Pavlowsky et al., 2018.

claim: Felsenberg et al., 2018 showed that MBON-γ1pedc>α/β directly inhibits an avoidance-driving MBON (MBON-γ5β′2a), such that its activity increases after punishment as the inhibition is released.
source: Felsenberg et al., 2018 further showed that the same MBON directly inhibits an avoidance-driving MBON (MBON-γ5β′2a), such that its activity increases (driving avoidance) after punishment as the inhibition is released.
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The model responses of PPL1-γ1pedc, MBON-γ1pedc, and MBON-γ5β′2a during aversive conditioning follow a similar pattern to experimental data.
source: Figure 5C–E shows the responses of these neurons from experimental data (left) and from our model (right) during aversive conditioning (the paradigm shown in Figure 4), which follow a similar pattern.
evidence: This is a comparison of model outputs with experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The response of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β to odour B drops sharply already from the second trial of the acquisition phase.
source: Learning in this circuit is shown by the sharp drop (in both experimental data and model) of the response of MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (Figure 5D) to odour B already from the second trial of the acquisition phase.
evidence: This is observed in both experimental data and model results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The rapid decrease in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β response is due to the depressing effect of the DAN on the KC→MBON synaptic weight.
source: This rapid decrease is due to the depressing effect of the DAN on the KC→MBON synaptic weight.
evidence: This is an inference from the model mechanism.

claim: If the unconditional stimulus occurs without the conditional stimulus, the MBON synaptic weights reset due to the recovery effect.
source: Note that we name this a 'discharging' DAN as the target synaptic strengths are high or 'charged' by default. However, due to our plasticity rule, if the unconditional stimuli (US) subsequently occurs without the CS (see unpaired phase in the model, for which we do not have experimental data), the MBON synaptic weights reset due to the recovery effect (see Figure 5—figure supplement 3A, odour B).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The susceptible memory is easily created and erased, consistent with high learning rate and low retention time observed in Aso and Rubin, 2016.
source: This is consistent with the high learning rate and low retention time observed in Aso and Rubin, 2016, and it results in a memory that is easily created and erased: a 'susceptible memory' (SM).
evidence: This is a comparison of model properties with experimental observations from cited work.

claim: The response of MBON-γ5β′2a has the opposite pattern to MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, starting to respond to odour B from the second trial of acquisition as it is no longer restrained.
source: The response of MBON-γ5β′2a (Figure 5E) can be observed to have the opposite pattern, that is, it starts to respond to odour B from the second trial of acquisition as it is no longer 'restrained'.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Experimental data shows a slight drop in the shock response of PPL1-γ1pedc during the whole experiment, although it remains active throughout.
source: In Figure 5C, the experimental data shows a slight drop in the shock response (first paired with odour B, then with odour A) of the DAN, PPL1-γ1pedc, during the whole experiment, although it remains active throughout.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The drop in DAN response may reflect sensory adaptation to shock.
source: We assume that this drop may reflect a sensory adaptation to shock but have not included it in our model.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the observed effect.

claim: The model shows a positive feedback effect where the DAN causes depression of the MBON response to odour, reducing inhibition of the DAN, which increases its response, causing even further depression in the MBON.
source: Consequently, the model data shows a positive feedback effect: the DAN causes depression of the MBON response to odour, reducing inhibition of the DAN, which increases its response, causing even further depression in the MBON.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: The positive feedback effect in the model is opposite to the expected effects of reward prediction error.
source: Note that this is opposite to the expected effects of reward prediction error.
evidence: This is a comparison of the model mechanism with RPE theory.

claim: Similar microcircuits to the susceptible and restrained memory circuits can be extracted from the connectome described in Aso et al., 2014a and Li et al., 2020.
source: Similar microcircuits in the MB can be extracted from the connectome described in Aso et al., 2014a and Li et al., 2020 (also identified in larvae; Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published connectome data.

claim: There are exactly corresponding susceptible and restrained memory microcircuits with opposite valence.
source: This leads us to the assumption that there are exactly corresponding susceptible and restrained memory microcircuits with opposite valence, that is, a reward-encoding DAN that discharges the response to odour of an avoidance-driving MBON, which in turn releases its restraint on an attraction-driving MBON (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and right side of the IC in Figure 3, which mirrors the left side, with opposite valence).
evidence: This is an inference from the connectome data and model structure.

claim: PAM-γ4<γ1γ2 is the reward-encoding discharging DAN in the opposite valence susceptible/restrained circuit.
source: We further suggest specific identities for the neurons forming this circuit: PAM-γ4<γ1γ2 as the reward-encoding discharging DAN; MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 as the avoidance-driving susceptible MBON; and MBON-γ2α'1 as the attraction-driving restrained MBON (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a proposed mapping of model components to identified neurons.

claim: MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 is the avoidance-driving susceptible MBON in the opposite valence susceptible/restrained circuit.
source: We further suggest specific identities for the neurons forming this circuit: PAM-γ4<γ1γ2 as the reward-encoding discharging DAN; MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 as the avoidance-driving susceptible MBON; and MBON-γ2α'1 as the attraction-driving restrained MBON (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a proposed mapping of model components to identified neurons.

claim: MBON-γ2α'1 is the attraction-driving restrained MBON in the opposite valence susceptible/restrained circuit.
source: We further suggest specific identities for the neurons forming this circuit: PAM-γ4<γ1γ2 as the reward-encoding discharging DAN; MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 as the avoidance-driving susceptible MBON; and MBON-γ2α'1 as the attraction-driving restrained MBON (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a proposed mapping of model components to identified neurons.

claim: The identification of MBON-γ2α'1 as attraction-driving restrained MBON is based on the possibility of inhibiting connections from MBONs in the γ4 compartment to the ones in the γ2 compartment suggested by Aso et al., 2019 and Cohn et al., 2015.
source: The latter identification is based on the possibility of inhibiting connections from MBONs in the γ4 compartment to the ones in the γ2 compartment suggested by Aso et al., 2019 and Cohn et al., 2015.
evidence: This is based on cited anatomical and functional studies.

claim: It is possible that MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 can inhibit MBON-γ2α′1 through glutamate-gated chloride channels.
source: Although MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 is characterised by the glutamate neurotransmitter, it is possible that it can inhibit MBON-γ2α′1 through glutamate-gated chloride channels (Cleland, 1996; Liu and Wilson, 2013; McCarthy et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms cited from the literature.

claim: McCurdy et al., 2021 suggest that MBON-γ2α′1 indirectly decreases the synaptic weights from KCs to MBON-γ5β′2a via PAM-β′2a.
source: McCurdy et al., 2021 suggest that the attraction-driving restrained MBON in the previous circuit (MBON-γ2α′1) indirectly decreases the synaptic weights from KCs to the avoidance-driving restrained MBON (MBON-γ5β′2a) via an attraction-encoding DAN (PAM-β′2a).
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The reciprocal short-term memories microcircuit is supported by Felsenberg et al., 2018 and Berry et al., 2018.
source: This microcircuit is also supported by Felsenberg et al., 2018 and Berry et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Cohn et al., 2015 and Li et al., 2020 suggest that MBON-γ5β′2a excites PPL1-γ2α′1.
source: Cohn et al., 2015 and Li et al., 2020 suggest that the corresponding avoidance-driving restrained MBON (MBON-γ5β′2a) excites an avoidance-encoding DAN (PPL1-γ2α′1), which closes the loop by affecting the KC connections to the attraction-driving restrained MBON, forming what we call the 'reciprocal short-term memories' microcircuit as shown in Figure 6A (actual neurons in the MBs) and Figure 6B (schematic representation of the described connections).
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The charging DANs should be activated directly by reinforcement as well as the restrained MBONs.
source: The 'charging' DANs, PAM-β′2a and PPL1-γ2α′1 (named after their long-term memory charging property, i.e., potentiation effect on another KC→MBON synapse, as we describe in the long-term memory microcircuit section), should be activated directly by reinforcement as well as the restrained MBONs.
evidence: This is a proposed property of the model.

claim: The activation of charging DANs by both reinforcement and restrained MBONs allows for memories to be affected directly by the reinforcement and by the expression of the opposite valence memories.
source: This allows for memories to be affected directly by the reinforcement, but also by the expression of the opposite valence memories.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model structure.

claim: The reciprocal short-term memories feature keeps the balance between the memories by automatically erasing a memory when a memory of the opposite valence starts building up.
source: The latter feature keeps the balance between the memories by automatically erasing a memory when a memory of the opposite valence starts building up and results in the balanced learning rate and retention time as observed in Aso and Rubin, 2016.
evidence: This is an inference about model function compared with experimental observations.

claim: The restrained MBONs store short-term memories because the memories in this pair are very fragile.
source: Because the memories in this pair of restrained MBONs are very fragile, we predict that these MBONs store short-term memories.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model properties.

claim: Ichinose et al., 2015 describe a microcircuit where a reward-encoding DAN (PAM-α1) potentiates the KC→MBON synapses of MBON-α1, and MBON-α1 in turn excites PAM-α1.
source: Ichinose et al., 2015 describe a microcircuit where a reward-encoding DAN (PAM-α1) potentiates the KC→MBON synapses of MBON-α1, and MBON-α1 in turn excites PAM-α1.
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Using data from Li et al., 2020, numerous similar microcircuits to the PAM-α1/MBON-α1 circuit were found, including MBONs with recurrent arrangement of connectivity to the charging DANs.
source: Using data from Li et al., 2020, we find numerous similar microcircuits, and in particular, MBONs that appear to have this recurrent arrangement of connectivity to the 'charging' DANs we have introduced to the circuit in the previous section.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published connectome data.

claim: PAM-β′2a can potentiate the response of the attraction-driving MBON-β2β′2a.
source: Specifically, we assume that the reward-encoding charging DAN (PAM-β′2a) can potentiate the response of the attraction-driving MBON-β2β′2a; and similarly the punishment-encoding charging DAN (PPL1-γ2α′1) potentiates the avoidance-driving MBON-α′1 (see Figure 7A and B; Figure 7C shows these connections schematically, with the KCs omitted for convenience).
evidence: This is a proposed mapping based on connectome data.

claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 potentiates the avoidance-driving MBON-α′1.
source: Specifically, we assume that the reward-encoding charging DAN (PAM-β′2a) can potentiate the response of the attraction-driving MBON-β2β′2a; and similarly the punishment-encoding charging DAN (PPL1-γ2α′1) potentiates the avoidance-driving MBON-α′1 (see Figure 7A and B; Figure 7C shows these connections schematically, with the KCs omitted for convenience).
evidence: This is a proposed mapping based on connectome data.

claim: The DAN-MBON connections in the LTM microcircuit form positive feedback circuits where the DAN potentiates the response of the MBON to the odour, which increases its excitation of the DAN.
source: Crucially, these connections form positive feedback circuits — the DAN potentiates the response of the MBON to the odour, which increases its excitation of the DAN.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: Even when the reinforcement ceases, the learning momentum can continue due to the saturation effect, resulting in long-term memory consolidation and enhancement.
source: As a consequence, even when the reinforcement ceases, the learning momentum can continue — this is the saturation effect of the learning rule (see Figure 2D) and results in long-term memory consolidation and enhancement.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The model shows charging of the avoidance-driving LTM MBON during acquisition and its continued increase during the forgetting phases.
source: Figure 7D (right) demonstrates the charging of the avoidance-driving LTM MBON during the acquisition (for odour B) and its continued increase during the forgetting phases.
evidence: This is shown in the model results in Figure 7D.

claim: The charging trends in the LTM MBON are not evident in the experimental data.
source: However, these trends are not evident in the experimental data as illustrated in Figure 7D (left).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Responses of LTM neurons depend on the overall experience of the animal and are thus hard to predict during one experiment.
source: We suggest this is because responses of LTM neurons depend on the overall experience of the animal and are thus hard to predict during one experiment.
evidence: This is speculation about why the model and data differ.

claim: Once the LTM microcircuit begins to charge, it will have a self-sustaining increase in the weights during odour delivery, preventing any subsequent adaptation to altered reward contingencies.
source: As described so far, once the LTM microcircuit begins to charge, it will have a self-sustaining increase in the weights during odour delivery, preventing any subsequent adaptation to altered reward contingencies.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The two LTM MBONs are connected via respective forgetting DANs to allow LTM weights to decrease in response to charging of the LTM of opposite valence.
source: To allow these weights to decrease, specifically, to decrease in response to charging of the LTM of opposite valence, we connect the two LTM MBONs via respective 'forgetting' DANs (see Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Forgetting DANs do not receive any direct reinforcement signals.
source: Note that these forgetting DANs do not receive any direct reinforcement signals.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: As long as an LTM MBON is active, its respective forgetting DAN is also active and causes synaptic depression for the opposite LTM MBON.
source: Instead, as long as an LTM MBON is active, its respective forgetting DAN is also active and causes synaptic depression for the opposite LTM MBON (forgetting the learnt memory; see Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Sustained reinforcement of one valence can gradually overcome the positive feedback of the LTM circuit of opposite valence, causing the charging momentum to drop and eventually negate.
source: As a consequence, sustained reinforcement of one valence can gradually overcome the positive feedback of the LTM circuit of opposite valence, causing the charging momentum to drop and eventually negate.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The LTMs are in long-term competition.
source: The LTMs are thus in long-term competition.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The reciprocal LTMs microcircuit has been identified in the descriptions of Aso et al., 2014a and Li et al., 2020.
source: We have identified the reciprocal LTMs microcircuit of Figure 8B in the descriptions of Aso et al., 2014a and Li et al., 2020, where MBON-α′1 is the avoidance-driving LTM MBON, MBON-β2β′2a is the attraction-driving LTM MBON, PAM-β2β′2a is the avoidance-driving forgetting DAN, and PPL1-γ2α′1 is the attraction-driving forgetting DAN, as shown in Figure 8A.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published connectome data.

claim: There is only one PPL1-γ2α′1 per hemisphere, which has been suggested as both the punishment-encoding charging DAN and the attraction-driving forgetting DAN.
source: One problem with this identification is that there is only one PPL1-γ2α′1 per hemisphere, and we have already suggested that it should be identified as the punishment-encoding charging DAN in our model.
evidence: This is a potential issue with the proposed mapping.

claim: There are multiple axon terminals of PPL1-γ2α′1 in the mushroom body and each one seems to communicate a different response.
source: However, there are multiple axon terminals of this neuron in the MB (e.g., MB296B1 and MB296B2) and each one of them seems to communicate a different response (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1, row 5, columns 6 and 7).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The responses communicated by the MB296B1 terminal are close to the ones produced by the punishment-encoding charging DAN.
source: Interestingly, the responses communicated by the MB296B1 terminal are close to the ones produced by the punishment-encoding charging DAN (see Figure 6C), and the ones of the MB296B2 are close to the ones produced by the attraction-driving forgetting DAN (see Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data with model predictions.

claim: Different axons of the same DA neuron might create responses that depend on where the axon terminates and actually work as separate processing units.
source: This implies that different axons of the same DA neuron might create responses that depend on where the axon terminates and actually work as separate processing units.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data.

claim: The reconstructed responses of the forgetting DANs from the model are surprisingly similar to the ones observed in the data.
source: Figure 8C and D shows that the reconstructed responses of these neurons from our model are surprisingly similar to the ones observed in the data.
evidence: This is a comparison of model outputs with experimental data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: The forgetting DANs suppress the KC synaptic weights of their respective restrained MBONs, forming the memory assimilation mechanism microcircuit.
source: We thus predict that the forgetting DANs also suppress the KC synaptic weights of their respective restrained MBONs, forming the 'memory assimilation mechanism' (MAM) microcircuit (see Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The memory assimilation mechanism effectively allows memory transfer between the restrained and the LTM MBONs, enhancing both the adaptability and the capacity of the circuit.
source: This effectively allows memory transfer between the restrained and the LTM MBONs, enhancing both the adaptability and the capacity of the circuit.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The depression effect of the forgetting DANs on the KC→restrained MBON synapses of the same valence is supported by Aso et al., 2014a.
source: The depression effect of the forgetting DANs on the KC→restrained MBON synapses of the same valence is supported by Aso et al., 2014a.
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: PAM-β2β′2a modulates the KC→MBON-γ5β′2a synapses.
source: More specifically, the avoidance-driving forgetting DAN we have identified as PAM-β2β′2a modulates the KC→MBON-γ5β′2a synapses, while for the attraction-driving forgetting DAN, PPL1-γ2α′1, modulates the KC→MBON-γ2α′1 synapses, as show in Figure 9A and B, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the connectome data cited from Aso et al., 2014a.

claim: PPL1-γ2α′1 modulates the KC→MBON-γ2α′1 synapses.
source: More specifically, the avoidance-driving forgetting DAN we have identified as PAM-β2β′2a modulates the KC→MBON-γ5β′2a synapses, while for the attraction-driving forgetting DAN, PPL1-γ2α′1, modulates the KC→MBON-γ2α′1 synapses, as show in Figure 9A and B, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the connectome data cited from Aso et al., 2014a.

claim: Simulated flies placed in a virtual arena with two odour gradients variously paired with reinforcements allow identification of different aspects of the produced behaviour and motivation.
source: Therefore, we further simulate the behaviour produced by the IC with simulated flies placed in a virtual arena, where they are exposed to two odour gradients, of different strengths, and variously paired with reinforcements. As we have full access to the neural responses, the synaptic weights, and the position of the simulated flies for every time-step, this allows us to identify different aspects of the produced behaviour and motivation, including the effect of the LTM on the behaviour and whether 'choice' occurs because the animal is attracted by one odour or repulsed by the other.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral simulation approach.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule allows the animal to express a variety of behaviours depending on their experience while remaining very simple.
source: The proposed DPR, while remaining very simple, allows the animal to express a variety of behaviours depending on their experience.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule remains local to the synapse, depending only on information plausibly available in the presynaptic area of the KC axon.
source: The rule remains local to the synapse, that is, it depends only on information that is plausibly available in the presynaptic area of the KC axon (Equation 1): the activity of the KC, the level of DA, and the deviation of the current 'weight' from a set-point 'resting weight'.
evidence: This is a description of the properties of the proposed rule.

claim: It was not possible to obtain good results without the third component (deviation from resting weight) in the dopaminergic plasticity rule.
source: We note that it was not possible to obtain good results without this third component to the rule, although the underlying biophysical mechanism is unknown; we speculate that it could involve synapsin as it has a direct role in regulating the balance of reserve and release vesicle pools, and is required in the MB for associative learning (Michels et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from model testing and speculation about the biological mechanism.

claim: The bidirectional dopaminergic factor is based on the results of Handler et al., 2019, who showed the combination of DopR1 and DopR2 receptor activity can result in depression or potentiation of the synapse.
source: The rule also introduces a bidirectional 'dopaminergic factor' based on the results of Handler et al., 2019, who showed the combination of DopR1 and DopR2 receptor activity can result in depression or potentiation of the synapse.
evidence: This is based on cited experimental work.

claim: The saturation effect allows LTM MBONs to consolidate their memories and makes it very hard to forget.
source: In particular, the saturation allows LTM MBONs to consolidate their memories and makes it very hard to forget.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the saturation effect.

claim: Only a persistent change in the valence of reinforcement experienced with a given stimuli can reset the activity of LTM MBONs through the reciprocal LTMs microcircuit.
source: This only occurs for consistently experienced associations, which then become strongly embedded. Only a persistent change in the valence of reinforcement experienced with a given stimuli can reset the activity of LTM MBONs through the reciprocal LTMs microcircuit, which equips the circuit with flexibility even in the LTMs.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The memory assimilation mechanism increases the capacity of the circuit by allowing restrained MBON learning to be eventually assimilated by the LTM MBONs.
source: Further, the fact that the DPR allows STMs (restrained) and LTMs to interact through the memory assimilation mechanism (MAM) increases the capacity of the circuit. Whatever the restrained MBONs learn is eventually assimilated by the LTM MBONs, opening up space for the formation of new memories in the restrained MBONs.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: When combined with sparse coding of odours in a large number of KCs, the LTM MBONs can store multiple memories for different odours.
source: When combined with sparse coding of odours in a large number of KCs, the LTM MBONs can store multiple memories for different odours.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: The reward prediction error plasticity rule lacks the flexibility of the dopaminergic plasticity rule and fails to maintain useful LTMs when applied to the same circuit architecture.
source: By contrast, the RPE plasticity rule lacks this flexibility and fails to maintain useful LTMs when applied to the same circuit architecture.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model results with RPE vs DPR.

claim: A literal interpretation of RPE for the mushroom body would require that the difference between the postsynaptic MBON activity and the DA level is calculated in the presynaptic KC axon.
source: A literal interpretation of RPE for the MB would require that the difference (error) between the postsynaptic MBON activity and the DA level is somehow calculated in the presynaptic KC axon.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements of RPE implementation.

claim: The literal interpretation of RPE seems inconsistent with the observation that learning is generally unaffected by silencing the MBONs during acquisition.
source: This seems inconsistent with the observation that learning is generally unaffected by silencing the MBONs during acquisition (Hige et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2007; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: The evidence for MBON-DAN feedback connections is well-grounded, but it is less clear that they are consistently opposing.
source: However, although the evidence for MBON-DAN feedback connections is well-grounded, it is less clear that they are consistently opposing.
evidence: This is an assessment of the evidence from the literature.

claim: Some DANs that depress synaptic weights receive inhibitory feedback from MBONs.
source: For example, in the microcircuits we have described, based on neurophysiological evidence, some DANs that depress synaptic weights receive inhibitory feedback from MBONs (Pavlowsky et al., 2018) and some DANs that potentiate synaptic weights receive excitatory feedback from DANs (Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited experimental work.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule is able to operate with a variety of MBON-DAN connections.
source: As we have shown, the DPR is able to operate with this variety of MBON-DAN connections.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results.

claim: By using the appropriate circuit with positive MBON-DAN feedback to depressing DANs, the dopaminergic plasticity rule could also have a reward prediction error effect.
source: Note that, by using the appropriate circuit, that is, positive MBON-DAN feedback to depressing DANs, our DPR could also have an RPE effect.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential of the proposed rule.

claim: The model supports backward (relief) conditioning results presented in Handler et al., 2019.
source: In the methods section 'Derivation of the dopaminergic plasticity rule', we demonstrate that our model supports the backward (or relief) conditioning results presented in Handler et al., 2019.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the methods section.

claim: Handler et al., 2019 suggest that backward conditioning is a mechanism driven by ER-Ca2+ and cAMP in a KC→MBON synapse when a single DAN releases DA on it.
source: Handler et al., 2019 suggest that the backward conditioning is a mechanism driven by ER-Ca2+ and cAMP in a KC→MBON synapse, when a single DAN releases DA on it.
evidence: This is a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: In the model, different time courses in the response of DopR1 and DopR2 receptors cause the different patterns of ER-Ca2+ and cAMP, resulting in opposite associations for forward and backward conditioning.
source: In our model, we assume that different time courses in the response of DopR1 and DopR2 receptors cause the different patterns of ER-Ca2+ and cAMP, resulting in the formation of opposite associations for forward and backward conditioning.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The backward conditioning effect in the model requires that the target MBON inhibits the respective DAN, altering the time course of neurotransmitter release.
source: We note however that in our model the effect also requires that the target MBON inhibits the respective DAN (as in our susceptible memory microcircuits) altering the time course of neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Backward conditioning may not occur in all mushroom body compartments.
source: This may suggest that backward conditioning does not occur in all MB compartments.
evidence: This is speculation based on the model mechanism.

claim: The mechanism for backward conditioning in the model is better supported than the hypothesised mechanism of post-inhibitory rebound in opposing valence DANs presented in Adel and Griffith, 2021.
source: We believe that this mechanism for backward conditioning is better supported than the hypothesised mechanism of post-inhibitory rebound in opposing valence DANs presented in Adel and Griffith, 2021, although some role for both mechanisms is possible.
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Unpaired conditioning involves the presentation of reinforcement and a specific odour in alternation with less temporal proximity.
source: Backward conditioning can be distinguished from the unpaired conditioning effect; the latter involves the presentation of reinforcement and a specific odour in alternation with less temporal proximity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about conditioning paradigms.

claim: Unpaired conditioning produces a change in response to the odour that is opposite in valence to the reinforcement.
source: It has been observed (Jacob and Waddell, 2020; Schleyer et al., 2018) that this procedure will produce a change in response to the odour that is opposite in valence to the reinforcement, for example, approach to an odour that is 'unpaired' with shock.
evidence: This is based on cited experimental observations.

claim: The model produces unpaired conditioning through a different mechanism than backward conditioning.
source: Surprisingly, our model also produces unpaired conditioning, notably through a different mechanism than backward conditioning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model results.

claim: When DANs are activated by a reinforcement without KC activation, the weights of all KCs are potentially altered.
source: When DANs are activated by a reinforcement without KC activation, the weights of all KCs are potentially altered, for example, restored towards their resting weight or slightly potentiated.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Subsequent presentation of odour alone can be accompanied by MBON-driven activation of DANs, resulting in specific alteration of the weights for the presented odour.
source: This alteration means that subsequent presentation of odour alone can be accompanied by MBON-driven activation of DANs, resulting in specific alteration of the weights for the presented odour.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: In the unpaired conditioning example, odour A starts to self-reinforce its attractive LTM when presented in alternation with shock and will be preferred to an alternative odour B in subsequent testing.
source: In the example of Figure 12, odour A starts to self-reinforce its attractive LTM when presented in alternation with shock and will be preferred to an alternative odour B in subsequent testing.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model results shown in Figure 12.

claim: Repeated presentation of other odours during testing without further shock might lead to generalisation (equal preference to all experienced odours).
source: However, repeated presentation of other odours during testing, without further shock, might lead to generalisation (equal preference to all experienced odours).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model mechanism.

claim: The self-reinforcing property of the positive feedback in the LTM microcircuit can account for second-order conditioning.
source: The self-reinforcing property of the positive feedback in the LTM microcircuit can also account for second-order conditioning.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequences of the model mechanism.

claim: If a motivation has been associated to an odour, MBONs related to that motivation will have increased activity when the odour is delivered, even in the absence of reinforcement.
source: If a motivation has been associated to an odour, MBONs related to that motivation will have increased activity when the odour is delivered, even in the absence of reinforcement.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: In the LTM microcircuit, the positive MBON-DAN connection will activate the charging DAN when a learned odour is presented, so any additional cue presented alongside will also experience an increase in the respective KC→MBON weights.
source: In the LTM microcircuit, the positive MBON-DAN connection will consequently activate the charging DAN, so any additional cue (or KC activity) presented alongside the learned odour will also experience an increase in the respective KC→MBON weights, creating a similar charging momentum and resulting in a second-order association.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Second-order conditioning might happen directly in the LTM microcircuit without being filtered by the susceptible and restrained memories first.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, this predicts that second-order conditioning might happen directly in the LTM microcircuit without being filtered by the susceptible and restrained memories first.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model mechanism.

claim: The prediction that second-order conditioning occurs directly in LTM would be consistent with the observation that second-order conditioning in flies requires strong induction of the first-order memory and that first-order memory does not appear to be extinguished by the absence of reinforcement during second-order training.
source: This would be consistent with the observation that second-order conditioning in flies requires strong induction of the first-order memory and that first-order memory does not appear to be extinguished by the absence of reinforcement during second-order training (Tabone and de Belle, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The dopaminergic plasticity rule would not produce blocking.
source: Finally, although we have not tested it explicitly here, it is clear that our plasticity rule (unlike RPE) would not produce blocking.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule.

claim: The blocking effect is when the conditioning to one stimulus subsequently blocks any conditioning to other elements of a mixture including that stimulus.
source: The blocking effect, as described by Kamin, 1967, is when the conditioning to one stimulus subsequently blocks any conditioning to other elements of a mixture including that stimulus.
evidence: This is a citation to established psychological theory.

claim: Under RPE learning, blocking is explained by the first stimulus already correctly predicting the reinforcer, so there is no error to drive a change in the weights.
source: Under RPE learning, this is explained by the first stimulus already correctly predicting the reinforcer, so there is no error to drive a change in the weights.
evidence: This is an explanation of RPE theory.

claim: Using the dopaminergic plasticity rule, the updates are local to the synapse and do not depend on a calculation of errors summarised across different odour identities, so blocking does not happen.
source: Using the DPR, the updates are local to the synapse and do not depend on a calculation of errors summarised across different odour identities, so blocking does not happen, which is consistent with the observed behaviour of fruit flies (Young et al., 2011; Brembs and Heisenberg, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the proposed rule compared with experimental observations.

claim: The model suggests that only KC→MBON, MBON⊣DAN, MBON→DAN, and DAN⊸MBON connections are essential for successful learning in the mushroom bodies.
source: Our model suggests that only KC→MBON, MBON⊣DAN, MBON→DAN, and DAN⊸MBON connections are essential for successful learning in the MBs.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results.

claim: There are additional known connections in the mushroom bodies, such as KC→APL, APL⊣KC, DAN→MBON, axoaxonic KC→KC and KC→DAN connections that have been neglected in this model.
source: However, there are a number of additional known connections in the MBs, such as KC→APL, APL⊣KC, DAN→MBON, axoaxonic KC→KC and KC→DAN connections that have been neglected in this model, and need further consideration.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations of the model.

claim: In the larval brain, there are two anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons, one for each mushroom body.
source: In the larval brain, there are two anterior paired lateral (APL) neurons, one for each MB.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: APL neurons extend their dendrites to the lobes of the mushroom bodies and terminate their axons in the calyxes releasing the inhibitory GABA neurotransmitter.
source: They extend their dendrites to the lobes of the MBs and terminate their axons in the calyxes releasing the inhibitory GABA neurotransmitter (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on cited anatomical studies.

claim: In the adult brain, both APL dendrites and axons innervate the calyx and the lobes, suggesting they function as both global and local inhibitory circuits.
source: Although there are still two of them, in the adult brain both their dendrites and axons are innervating the calyx and the lobes (Wu et al., 2013), suggesting that they function as both global and local inhibitory circuits.
evidence: This is based on cited anatomical studies and inference about function.

claim: DAN⊣APL and APL⊣DAN connections have been proposed, but there is no clear description of what their function is.
source: Moreover, DAN⊣APL (Liu and Davis, 2009) and APL⊣DAN (Wu et al., 2012) connections have been proposed, but there is no clear description of what their function is.
evidence: This is based on cited studies and an assessment of the literature.

claim: A potential function for the global/local inhibition network involving APL is gain control such that the total number of KCs firing to different stimuli remains similar.
source: Several previous models (Peng and Chittka, 2017; Delahunt et al., 2018) have demonstrated that a potential function for this global/local inhibition network is gain control such that the total number of KCs firing to different stimuli remains similar, and indeed that the same effect can be implemented using a flexible threshold for KC firing (Saumweber et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited modeling studies.

claim: The model simplified the KC input, representing just two odours as different patterns across a small number of KCs with a fixed number of them being active at all times, so the hypothesised gain control function of the APL is not useful.
source: In our model, we have simplified the KC input, representing just two odours as different patterns across a small number of KCs with a fixed number of them being active at all times, so the hypothesised gain control function of the APL is not useful here.
evidence: This is a description of the model simplification.

claim: It remains an interesting question whether there is learning between the KC and APL in the lobes, or between the APL and KC in the calyx, and what role this might play in the overall dynamics of memory acquisition.
source: However, it remains an interesting question whether there is learning between the KC and APL in the lobes (Zhou et al., 2019), or between the APL and KC in the calyx, and what role this might play in the overall dynamics of memory acquisition.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms not included in the model.

claim: Eichler et al., 2017 suggest that most of the KCs input (60%) is from other KCs.
source: In addition, Eichler et al., 2017 suggest that most of the KCs input, that is, 60%, is from other KCs.
evidence: This is a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: KC-KC connections together with APL connections might create local winner-takes-all networks that force a limited number of KCs per compartment to be active at one time.
source: We suggest that these connections (together with the ones from the APL) might create local winner-takes-all (WTA) networks that force a limited number of KCs per compartment to be active at one time.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of these connections.

claim: It is possible for the same KC axon to be active in one compartment but inactive in another.
source: This predicts that it is possible for the same KC axon to be active in one compartment but inactive in another (consistent with recent data from Bilz et al., 2020), and that an almost fixed number of KCs might be active at all times, even when no odour is delivered (e.g., fresh air only) enabling the acquisition and forgetting at all times.
evidence: This is a prediction from the proposed mechanism that is consistent with cited data.

claim: Ito et al., 2008 show that KCs can be active even in the absence of odours but with no consistent spiking, which is a characteristic of winner-takes-all networks when the underlying distribution of spikes across the neurons is almost uniform.
source: Ito et al., 2008 show that KCs can be active even in the absence of odours but with no consistent spiking, which is a characteristic of WTA networks when the underlying distribution of spikes across the neurons is almost uniform.
evidence: This is a citation to experimental observations and an inference about their interpretation.

claim: Eichler et al., 2017 observed that within a compartment, in a 'canonical microcircuit', KCs make direct synapses to the axons of DANs, and that DAN pre-synapses often simultaneously contact KCs and MBONs.
source: Eichler et al., 2017 also observed (from electron microscopy reconstruction in larva) that within a compartment, in a 'canonical microcircuit', KCs make direct synapses to the axons of DANs, and that DAN pre-synapses often simultaneously contact KCs and MBONs.
evidence: This is a citation to anatomical observations.

claim: The same KC→DAN and DAN→KC/MBON connections observed in larva have been observed in adult Drosophila by Takemura et al., 2017.
source: The same connections have been observed in adult Drosophila by Takemura et al., 2017.
evidence: This is a citation to anatomical observations.

claim: The extent to which KCs might be directly exciting DANs remains unclear.
source: The extent to which KCs (and thus odour inputs) might be directly exciting DANs remains unclear.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 show that stimulating KCs results in increased DAN responses and that DANs are activated through the ACh neurotransmitter.
source: Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 show that stimulating KCs results in increased DAN responses and that DANs are activated through the ACh neurotransmitter.
evidence: This is a citation to experimental observations.

claim: In the model, the effect of KC stimulation on DAN responses could be explained without assuming a direct connection, for example through the LTM microcircuit where activating KCs increases LTM MBON activity, which excites the charging DAN.
source: However, we note that in our model such an effect could be explained without assuming a direct connection. For example, in the LTM microcircuit, activating the KCs results in increased activity of the LTM MBON, which excites the respective charging DAN.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation based on the model mechanism.

claim: The DAN that Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 provide evidence from is PPL1-α2α′2, which gets excited by MBON-α2α′2 neurons as it is characterised by the ACh neurotransmitter.
source: The DAN that Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017 provide evidence from is PPL1-α2α′2, which gets excited by MBON-α2α′2 neurons as it is characterised by the ACh neurotransmitter (Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is based on cited anatomical and functional data.

claim: In model terms, MBON-α2α′2 could be an LTM MBON that excites its respective charging DAN, PPL1-α2α′2, and provide the source of ACh detected on it.
source: In our terms, this could be an LTM MBON that excites its respective charging DAN, PPL1-α2α′2 (Li et al., 2020), and provide the source of ACh detected on it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cited data in terms of the model.

claim: The altered activity of DANs in response to odours that have been observed during learning can be observed in the model without requiring direct KC→DAN connections or their modification.
source: More generally, the altered activity of DANs in response to odours that have been observed during learning can be also observed in our model, without requiring direct KC→DAN connections or their modification.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's ability to explain observations without additional mechanisms.

claim: Direct KC→DAN connections may possibly play a role in enhancing the specificity of dopamine-induced changes in KC→MBON connectivity.
source: Nevertheless, such connections may possibly play a role in enhancing the specificity of dopamine-induced changes in KC→MBON connectivity.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential function of these connections.

claim: The depression of KC→DAN synapses, in parallel with KC→MBON synapses, could provide an alternative mechanism for implementing RPE learning.
source: Interestingly, the depression of KC→DAN synapses, in parallel with KC→MBON synapses, could provide an alternative mechanism for implementing RPE learning (Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism based on cited anatomical observations.

claim: Takemura et al., 2017 demonstrate that the direct synapses from DANs to MBONs are functional in altering the MBON postsynaptic current to DAN activation, independently of KCs.
source: Takemura et al., 2017 demonstrate that the direct synapses observed from DANs to MBONs are functional in altering the MBON postsynaptic current to DAN activation, independently of KCs.
evidence: This is a citation to experimental observations.

claim: DAN→MBON synapses could be a mechanism by which learnt responses to reinforcements are coordinated with the current presence or absence of the reinforcement.
source: This could be a mechanism by which learnt responses to reinforcements are coordinated with the current presence or absence of the reinforcement (Schleyer et al., 2020; Schleyer et al., 2011; Gerber and Hendel, 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about the function of these connections based on cited work.

claim: Postsynaptic as well as presynaptic changes might be involved in learning at the KC→MBON synapse.
source: Another possibility is that postsynaptic as well as presynaptic changes might be involved in learning at the KC→MBON synapse (Pribbenow et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms based on cited work.

claim: The incentive circuit consists of six MBONs and six DANs that link a pair of antagonistic motivations, attraction, and avoidance.
source: The IC consists of six MBONs and six DANs that link a pair of antagonistic motivations, attraction, and avoidance.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: There are approximately 34 MBONs and approximately 130 DANs in the mushroom body of the adult fruit fly brain.
source: However, there are ∼34 MBONs and ∼130 DANs in the MB of the adult fruit fly brain, within which the IC is an identifiable motif.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The incentive circuit motif could be repeated, representing additional opposing motivations, with some neurons having multiple roles depending on the motivational context.
source: We suggest the possibility that this motif could be repeated, representing additional opposing motivations, with some neurons having multiple roles depending on the motivational context as proposed by Cohn et al., 2015, working either as restrained MBONs and discharging DANs, or as LTM MBONs and forgetting DANs depending on the reinforcer identity.
evidence: This is speculation about how the model could be extended, based on cited work.

claim: PAM-β2β′2a is a sugar-encoding discharging DAN in the appetitive olfactory conditioning context, but it also is an avoidance-driving forgetting DAN in a different context.
source: This could explain how PAM-β2β′2a (i.e., MB301B; May et al., 2020) is a sugar-encoding discharging DAN in the appetitive olfactory conditioning context, but it also is an avoidance-driving forgetting DAN in a different context (e.g., aversive olfactory conditioning).
evidence: This is an interpretation of cited experimental observations in terms of the model.

claim: Two MBONs of the incentive circuit do not interact with the α′/β′ KCs of the mushroom body.
source: In addition, two MBONs of the IC do not interact with the α′/β′ KCs of the MB.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β are part of two autonomous microcircuits (the susceptible memories) and work under the context provided by the approximately 675 γ-KCs relative to the task.
source: MBON-γ4>γ1γ2 and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β are part of two autonomous microcircuits, that is, the SMs, and are working under the context provided by the ∼675 γ-KCs relative to the task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model structure and function.

claim: It is possible that the KCs from the γ lobe connect to all the susceptible memories of the flies for the approximately eight available motivations.
source: This makes it possible that the KCs from the γ lobe connect to all the SMs of the flies for the approximately eight available motivations illustrated in Appendix 1—figure 1.
evidence: This is speculation about how the model could be extended.

claim: From a functional point of view, the mushroom bodies seem to be involved in the motivation and behaviour of the animal, especially when it comes to behaviours essential for survival.
source: From a functional point of view, the MBs seem to be involved in the motivation and behaviour of the animal, especially when it comes to behaviours essential for survival.
evidence: This is an inference about the function of the mushroom bodies.

claim: In the mammalian brain, motivation and behaviour essential for survival is subserved by the limbic system, which is composed of structures such as the thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala.
source: In the mammalian brain, this function is subserved by the limbic system, which is composed of a set of complicated structures, such as the thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, and amygdala (Dalgleish, 2004; Roxo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian neuroanatomy.
